anyway here’s a steak recipe: To cook a great steak at home, use a heavy cast-iron skillet to get a dark crust while keeping the inside tender and juicy. Ingredients • 1 thick-cut steak (like Ribeye or New York Strip, about 1.5 inches thick) • 1 tablespoon high-heat oil (like vegetable or canola oil) • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter • 2–3 garlic cloves, smashed • Fresh herbs (like rosemary or thyme) Instructions 1. Prep the Meat • Take the steak out of the fridge and let it rest on the counter for 20 to 30 minutes to reach room temperature. • Pat the steak completely dry with paper towels so it sears well and does not splatter oil. • Season both sides and the edges generously with salt and pepper, pressing the seasoning into the meat. 2. Sear the Steak • Place a cast-iron skillet over high heat until it is very hot and starts to smoke slightly. • Add the oil to the pan. • Lay the steak in the pan carefully, putting it down away from you so oil does not splash. • Sear the first side for 2 to 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms, then flip. 3. Butter Baste • Lower the heat to medium. • Add the butter, smashed garlic cloves, and fresh herbs to the pan. • Tilt the pan slightly and use a spoon to scoop the melted, foaming butter over the top of the steak continuously. • Cook until the internal temperature reaches about 5°F below your target doneness (125°F for medium-rare). 4. Rest and Serve • Remove the steak from the pan and place it on a cutting board or wire rack. • Let it rest loosely covered with foil for 5 to 10 minutes so the juices stay inside the meat. • Slice the steak across the grain and serve.

For those who don't know: What is grass? Grass consists of low, green, non-woody flowering plants belonging mainly to the true grass family, Poaceae, alongside similar plants like sedges and rushes. They feature narrow leaves with parallel veins, hollow jointed stems, and fibrous root systems that grow from the base rather than the tip. *Physical Structure* • Stems (Culms): Round and usually hollow between solid joints or nodes. • Leaves: Split into a lower sheath wrapped around the stem and an upper flattened blade. • Roots: Extensive underground fibrous networks that anchor the plant and prevent soil loss. • Growth habit: Grows from the base, allowing survival and rapid recovery after being cut, burned, or grazed. *Types and Habitats* • True grasses (Poaceae): Includes over 10,000 species such as lawn turf, bamboos, and major cereal crops like wheat, rice, and corn. • Grass-like families: Includes sedges (Cyperaceae) and rushes (Juncaceae) which prefer wet or marshy areas. • Global presence: Grasslands cover over 40% of the Earth's land surface, thriving in fields, plains, and varied climates.

anyway here’s a steak recipe: To cook a great steak at home, use a heavy cast-iron skillet to get a dark crust while keeping the inside tender and juicy. Ingredients • 1 thick-cut steak (like Ribeye or New York Strip, about 1.5 inches thick) • 1 tablespoon high-heat oil (like vegetable or canola oil) • Kosher salt and freshly ground black pepper • 2 tablespoons unsalted butter • 2–3 garlic cloves, smashed • Fresh herbs (like rosemary or thyme) Instructions 1. Prep the Meat • Take the steak out of the fridge and let it rest on the counter for 20 to 30 minutes to reach room temperature. • Pat the steak completely dry with paper towels so it sears well and does not splatter oil. • Season both sides and the edges generously with salt and pepper, pressing the seasoning into the meat. 2. Sear the Steak • Place a cast-iron skillet over high heat until it is very hot and starts to smoke slightly. • Add the oil to the pan. • Lay the steak in the pan carefully, putting it down away from you so oil does not splash. • Sear the first side for 2 to 3 minutes until a deep brown crust forms, then flip. 3. Butter Baste • Lower the heat to medium. • Add the butter, smashed garlic cloves, and fresh herbs to the pan. • Tilt the pan slightly and use a spoon to scoop the melted, foaming butter over the top of the steak continuously. • Cook until the internal temperature reaches about 5°F below your target doneness (125°F for medium-rare). 4. Rest and Serve • Remove the steak from the pan and place it on a cutting board or wire rack. • Let it rest loosely covered with foil for 5 to 10 minutes so the juices stay inside the meat. • Slice the steak across the grain and serve.

For those who don't know: What is grass? Grass consists of low, green, non-woody flowering plants belonging mainly to the true grass family, Poaceae, alongside similar plants like sedges and rushes. They feature narrow leaves with parallel veins, hollow jointed stems, and fibrous root systems that grow from the base rather than the tip. *Physical Structure* • Stems (Culms): Round and usually hollow between solid joints or nodes. • Leaves: Split into a lower sheath wrapped around the stem and an upper flattened blade. • Roots: Extensive underground fibrous networks that anchor the plant and prevent soil loss. • Growth habit: Grows from the base, allowing survival and rapid recovery after being cut, burned, or grazed. *Types and Habitats* • True grasses (Poaceae): Includes over 10,000 species such as lawn turf, bamboos, and major cereal crops like wheat, rice, and corn. • Grass-like families: Includes sedges (Cyperaceae) and rushes (Juncaceae) which prefer wet or marshy areas. • Global presence: Grasslands cover over 40% of the Earth's land surface, thriving in fields, plains, and varied climates.
